title: iac-bench 2026-10 Methodology
summary: How the iac-bench 2026-10 results were produced: the briefs, the evaluation setup, mechanical scoring against real tofu plans, the calibrated LLM judge, statistics and limitations.
body_markdown:
**Release 2026-10 · run 2026-10-22, judged 2026-10-23**


This document describes how the 2026-10 iac-bench results were produced: what the models were asked to do, how their output was scored, how the scores were aggregated, and what the numbers cannot tell you. The results are in[the 2026-10 results article](https://www.massdriver.cloud/blogs/iac-bench-2026-10-results) . Every scored item is defined in[the scoring criteria reference](https://www.massdriver.cloud/blogs/iac-bench-2026-10-scoring-criteria) .


## 1. Goals and scope


iac-bench measures how well a language model writes **reusable infrastructure-as-code modules** for OpenTofu (the open-source Terraform fork). A model gets a short request of the kind a platform engineer receives from a colleague, and must deliver a module another team could adopt.


Producing configuration that plans is the minimum. The benchmark measures what a senior reviewer would look for:


- Is the module secure without being asked?
- Does it protect data from accidental loss?
- Does it give its audience the right controls, and no more?
- Does it encode service-specific expertise?
- Is it built the way experienced module authors build modules?


The 2026-10 release covers **module generation only** , on three fixtures, one per major cloud.


## 2. Task design


### 2.1 Fixtures


Fixture Cloud and service Audience named in the brief Interface budget


G001 AWS · S3 bucket Application developers who "fill in a couple of obvious inputs" 8 inputs (zero credit at 16)


G002 GCP · Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL A DBA team that "knows PostgreSQL and Cloud SQL deeply" 25 inputs (zero credit at 35)


G003 Azure · App Service (Linux, containers) An SRE team that "knows Azure well" 20 inputs (zero credit at 30)


Each fixture is defined by a brief, a rubric, and a reference matrix. All three are published in the repository under` fixtures/generation/` and` testdata/solutions/` .


### 2.2 Briefs: measuring what the model volunteers


Briefs are short, realistic requests of two to five sentences. They state what is needed, who will use it, and the one or two facts about the environment that settle the design: for G002, that each environment already has its own VPC with private services access, and that every engineer and workload has a Google identity.


Briefs **do not list security, durability, or hygiene requirements.** Real requests rarely do, and listing them would turn the most valuable signal (does the model know to do these things?) into an instruction-following check. The rubric's criteria are therefore hidden from the model, but each core criterion is held to a rule: it must follow either from the brief or from practice that is universal for the service. A model is never penalized for failing to guess a preference the brief leaves open. Service-specific touches that go beyond universal practice are scored separately as *expertise* (§4.3).


### 2.3 Evaluation setup


Each model works as a tool-using agent in an isolated working directory, using the[Inspect](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/) framework. Every model gets the same system prompt (` prompts/generate-module.md` ), the same tools, and the same limits.


Setting Value


Tools` list_files` ,` read_file` ,` write_file` ,` tofu_validate` ,` tofu_plan` ,` tofu_fmt` ,` submit`


Deliverable A root module (` *.tf` ) plus` minimal.tfvars` , which gives a literal value for every variable without a default and must plan cleanly


Remote modules Not allowed (calling one fails the evaluation); local submodules allowed


Limits 150 messages, 30 minutes wall clock per attempt


API retries Up to 3 per request, then the attempt ends as an error (none occurred)


Planning` tofu plan` against real cloud accounts (AWS, GCP, Azure sandboxes). Nothing is ever applied.


OpenTofu 1.12.5


Providers Each module's own version constraints, resolved at run time


The` tofu_plan` tool plans against the same real cloud accounts used for scoring, so a model can verify that its module plans before submitting.


### 2.4 Models and settings


Model API identifier Access Weights


Claude Opus 5.5` claude-opus-5-5` Anthropic API Closed


Claude Fable 5.1` claude-fable-5-1` Anthropic API Closed


Claude Sonnet 5.5` claude-sonnet-5-5` Anthropic API Closed


Claude Haiku 5.5` claude-haiku-5-5` Anthropic API Closed


GPT-6 Astra` gpt-6-astra` OpenAI API (Responses) Closed


GPT-6 Luna` gpt-6-luna` OpenAI API (Responses) Closed


Gemini 3.1 Pro` gemini-3.1-pro-preview` Google Gemini API Closed


Gemini 3.6 Flash` gemini-3.6-flash` Google Gemini API Closed


Kimi K3` moonshotai/kimi-k3` OpenRouter Open


DeepSeek V4 Pro` deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro-0813` OpenRouter Open


All models ran with their providers' default sampling and reasoning settings. No temperature, reasoning-effort, or token-budget overrides were set. The GPT-6 models were called through OpenAI's Responses API, because its Chat Completions API rejects tool use combined with reasoning for these models. It changes only the API used, and no model setting.


**Pinning.** Except for DeepSeek V4 Pro (` -0813` ), the providers' APIs returned these identifiers as undated aliases, and none reported a dated snapshot. Results are therefore tied to the run date: all generations ran on **2026-10-22** , and all judging on **2026-10-23** . Hosted models can change behind an alias without notice.


### 2.5 Sampling


Each model ran each fixture **three times** , as independent attempts with no shared state: 10 models × 3 fixtures × 3 samples = **90 attempts** . Every attempt is scored and published. No attempt was re-run, discarded, or chosen after the fact.


## 3. Scoring overview


Each attempt passes through four layers.


Layer What it measures Nature Weight


1. Gate The module plans as a root module with its own` minimal.tfvars` Mechanical, pass/fail Prerequisite for layer 2


2. Rubric and expertise Fixture-specific consequences: security, data protection, audience fit, service expertise Mechanical, itemized and weighted 70%


3. Judge Design and craft against a published quality doctrine LLM judge, calibrated against a human 30%


4. Statistics Inputs, SLOC, tokens, time, estimated cost Mechanical, descriptive 0% (reported only)


**Composite = 0.70 × mechanical + 0.30 × judge grade** , on a 0–100 scale.


## 4. Mechanical scoring


### 4.1 The gate


The runner keeps only the variables that have no default from the model's own` minimal.tfvars` , then runs` tofu plan` on the module as a root module. A module that does not plan **fails the gate** :


- its rubric and expertise scores are 0;
- it is still graded by the judge, which keeps its grade (see §6.3);
- the failure is flagged ✗ in every results table.


### 4.2 The rubric


Each fixture's` rubric.yaml` declares weighted items, checked by a declarative check engine (` docs/generation-check-engine.md` ). The engine never looks at variable names. It evaluates outcomes in two places:


- **The plan.** Resources and attribute values in the defaults plan, and in the perturbation sweep described below.
- **The source.** Whether a value is a literal or flows from an input, traced through locals,` count` /` for_each` , dynamic blocks and` each.*` .


**The perturbation sweep.** For every documented input, the runner plans the module once more with that one input changed: booleans flipped, and enumerated values from` contains()` validations tried (up to five alternatives). The sweep reveals what an input actually controls without the engine knowing what the model named it. A setting reached through a direct toggle, a value inferred from an environment, or a derived local all score the same. Collection-typed and free-string inputs are not perturbed.


**The solver.** When an item fails at defaults and in the sweep, a solver reads the module's source and searches for inputs that would reach the item: up to three inputs changed at once, with values drawn from the module's own comparisons, validations and map keys, plus a few well-formed sample values per fixture (such as a resource ID). Inputs that would fail a validation or precondition are rejected. The runner then plans each proposed input set, and only a successful plan that shows the item counts. The source proposes and the plan decides.


Items take one of five **postures** , depending on what the item protects:


Posture Meaning Passes when


Hardcoded Security posture. An input that can weaken it is the defect, even if the default is safe. Every value the source can produce is secure (a literal, or an input confined to secure values, such as a choice between two encrypted modes), the resource exists unconditionally, and it stays secure in every sweep plan


On by default Safe by default, with a legitimate reason to turn it off On at defaults with a real way to turn it off. Always-on with no opt-out earns partial credit (0.75); off by default but reachable earns 0.5.


Offered A capability the audience should be able to reach Present at defaults or in at least one sweep plan


Graded Better and worse mechanisms that both work Credit for the best mechanism present


Budget Interface size fits the audience Full credit at or under the soft count, falling linearly to zero at the hard count


Items are grouped by role:


- **H items:** core security, durability and operability.
- **A items:** audience fit, covering exposure, restraint and the budget.
- **B items:** baseline items applied to every fixture: provider version constraints and descriptions.


Two H items per fixture are **mandatory** : the most severe security failure modes. Failing one is a **security finding** (⚠). It does not cap the score, but it marks the attempt unshippable.


### 4.3 Expertise items


Each fixture also lists **expertise items** . These are service-specific touches an experienced engineer adds without being asked, such as S3 bucket-owner-enforced ownership or IAM database authentication on Cloud SQL. They are checked mechanically and pooled into the mechanical score at weight 1 each, against rubric weights of 2–18. The rubric therefore decides whether a module meets the bar, and expertise separates modules that do.


Expertise items come from observation. Candidates come from differences between models and from the judge's rationales. Each is approved by the doctrine owner and records where it came from. An item must not reward inventing requirements the brief never stated.


### 4.4 The mechanical score


mechanical = (Σ rubric weight × credit + Σ expertise credit) / (Σ rubric weight + number of expertise items)


The rubric weight totals are 86 (G001), 97 (G002) and 72 (G003), including the baseline items. Each fixture has 7–9 expertise items.


### 4.5 Validating the rubric: the reference matrix


Each fixture ships hand-written reference modules that the rubric must classify correctly:


- **Two good designs** must score at least 0.95:


- ` ref_lean` is opinionated, with few inputs and choices inferred from a concept such as environment.
- ` ref_flexible` is more configurable.


- **Several deliberately bad designs** must fail the specific items each was built to fail:


- ` bad_passthrough` : every setting is an input.
- ` bad_minimal` : a bare resource.
- ` bad_unsafe` : one critical setting is exposed as an input.
- G003 also has` bad_open_slot` : a locked-down app with an open deployment slot.


The self-test runs this matrix against real cloud plans. If a deliberately good design fails the rubric, the rubric is wrong. The matrix exists so that the rubric rewards outcomes rather than one author's preferred shape.


## 5. The judge


### 5.1 What it grades


The judge is **Claude Opus 5.5** . It grades each module against the benchmark's quality doctrine (` docs/good-opentofu.md` , edition` af3ae1dd9fdc1c0c` ) on **14 sections** , scoring each 0 (no credit), 1 (partial) or 2 (full):


- **Weight 3:** Sensitive values.
- **Weight 2:** Interface design, Variables and validation, Scope.
- **Weight 1:** Internal logic, Inline vs separate resources, Outputs, Iteration (` for_each` vs` count` ), Data sources vs inputs, File layout, Lifecycle meta-arguments, Documentation, Deprecated and escape-hatch patterns, Anti-patterns.


The weighted mean is scaled to 0–100.


**The judge grades only what the rubric cannot.** The doctrine sections the rubric already scores are given to the judge as context but are not graded: insecure configurations, destructive defaults, unstated assumptions, tagging, versions, and provider declarations. A defect therefore never costs a module in both components.


**Blind to authorship.** The judge sees the brief, the doctrine, and the module's files: HCL first, then tfvars, then documentation. It never sees which model wrote the module. The files are marked as untrusted data, so instructions inside a module are not followed.


**Sampling.** Each module is graded three times independently. Each section takes the median of the three grades, and the judge returns one sentence of evidence per grade.


### 5.2 Calibration


A judge grade counts toward the composite only after the judge is calibrated against the doctrine owner (the human who maintains the doctrine), fixture by fixture:


1. For one fixture, the judge grades 8 modules: 6 from models and the 2 references. The modules are shown under blind labels.
2. The doctrine owner records their own grade (0, 1 or 2) for every section of every module: 112 cells. They see the judge's grade and evidence beside each cell.
3. Agreement is the share of cells where the judge's grade exactly matches the human's, computed per section. The judge is calibrated only if **every section matches on at least 6 of 8 modules** . The gate is per section so that easy sections cannot carry a judge through hard ones.


A second judge (GPT-5.5) graded the same modules during calibration. The doctrine owner reviewed in detail the cells where the two judges disagreed. Agreement for Claude Opus 5.5:


Fixture Cells Exact agreement Lowest section


G001 112 0.929 0.75 (Interface design, Scope, File layout, Documentation)


G002 112 0.973 0.875 (Interface design, File layout, Documentation)


G003 112 0.982 0.75 (Documentation)


GPT-5.5 failed the gate on G001 (Interface design) and G003 (Documentation, Sensitive values). A single judge is used across all fixtures, so that grades are comparable between fixtures.


**The final modules.** The 2026-10 modules were graded with the same judge model, judge code, doctrine edition and sampling as the calibration. Calibration was carried over on that basis; the doctrine owner did not re-review the final modules. Each grade file records where its calibration came from.


### 5.3 Known judge risks


- **Self-preference.** The judge and four of the ten candidates come from the same vendor. Blinding hides the author's name but not the author's style. An authorship test, which told the judge a fixed model had written every module, found no grade shift for the name. It does not rule out a preference for a familiar style. Finding 3 of the[results](https://www.massdriver.cloud/blogs/iac-bench-2026-10-results) shows the ranking with and without the judge.
- **Plan blindness.** The judge reads source and does not run` tofu plan` . It can miss a setting that the source omits and the provider defaults insecurely, and it can grade a module that does not plan. The rubric covers both cases. The two components are meant to complement each other.
- **Documentation accuracy is judged strictly.** Under the doctrine, any wrong or outdated statement earns 0 for Documentation, however small.


## 6. Aggregation and statistics


### 6.1 From attempts to scores


1. **Per attempt:** composite = 70 × mechanical + 0.30 × judge grade.
2. **Per model and fixture:** the median of the three attempts' composites, reported with the minimum–maximum range.
3. **Overall:** the mean of the three fixture medians, so each fixture counts equally.


Within a fixture the median is used, so one broken attempt out of three is reported as one broken attempt instead of being averaged into a result that hides it.


### 6.2 Uncertainty


Three samples per cell is a small sample, so the overall score is reported with a **bootstrap 95% confidence interval** :


- 10,000 resamples.
- Each model's three attempts per fixture are resampled with replacement, then the overall statistic is recomputed.


Each model also gets a **rank interval** : the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of its rank across joint bootstrap draws, following the LMArena convention. A ranking claim is made only where intervals separate. Pairwise win probabilities are published in the data release.


With n = 3, the bootstrap is coarse, and intervals are wide for models with one outlier attempt. Read them as a statement of how far the data supports a ranking, not as precise coverage.


### 6.3 Gate failures and findings


A module that fails the gate keeps its judge grade, so its composite is about 25–30 rather than 0. It is flagged ✗ and counted in the results tables. The judge grade is kept because the judge grades design and craft, which a plan failure does not erase. The flag shows that the attempt was unshippable. Security findings are handled the same way: flagged ⚠ and counted, but no score cap.


### 6.4 Cost and run statistics


Estimated cost per attempt uses list prices from OpenRouter, dated 2026-10-23, for every model, including closed models routed through their own APIs. Cache reads are charged at 0.1× and cache writes at 1.25× the input price. Judge calls are excluded. Token counts, wall-clock time, SLOC and input counts come from the eval logs. None of them affects any score.


## 7. Limitations


- **Plan-only.** Nothing is applied. Errors that only appear at apply time, idempotency, and destroy behavior are not measured.
- **Three services.** One service per cloud does not represent the breadth of infrastructure work, and results should not be generalized beyond these fixtures.
- **Small samples.** Three attempts per model and fixture. Neighboring models in the results frequently cannot be told apart, and the tables say so.
- **One scaffold.** Scores measure a model inside this scaffold and prompt. A different agent scaffold could produce different results.
- **Sweep coverage.** The sweep changes one input at a time and does not perturb collections or free-form strings. The solver reaches further, but it only models part of the language and draws values from the module's source and a few samples, so a capability that needs a list to be populated or a value of an unusual shape can go undetected. A defect that appears only when a collection input is populated (for example, a databases input that breaks the plan once used) is not caught by the rubric. The judge sometimes catches it.
- **Public fixtures.** Briefs, rubrics, references and the doctrine are public and may enter future training data. Rising scores on these fixtures without corroboration from held-out variants should be read as contamination.
- **Opinionated doctrine.** The judged 30% encodes one organization's documented preferences. Per-section grades are published so a reader can discard any section they disagree with, and the mechanical score is reported on its own.


## 8. Disclosure


iac-bench is developed by Massdriver, which builds infrastructure tooling. Massdriver wrote the briefs, rubrics, references and doctrine, and its staff acted as the calibrating human.


## 9. Reproducibility and data


The results were scored by the code tagged[2026-10](https://github.com/massdriver-cloud/iac-bench/tree/2026-10) in the repository. At that tag, the repository contains everything needed to reproduce or audit a score:


- **Evaluation code:**` src/iacbench/` .
- **Prompt:**` prompts/generate-module.md` .
- **Fixtures, rubrics and references:**` fixtures/` and` testdata/` .
- **Doctrine:**` docs/good-opentofu.md` .
- **Scoring policy:**` composite-scoring-policy.yaml` .
- **Price snapshot:**` prices.yaml` .


The[2026-10 data release](https://github.com/massdriver-cloud/iac-bench/tree/2026-10/results/2026-10) (` results/2026-10/` in the repository) contains:


- the 30 eval logs holding all 90 attempts' transcripts;
- the 90 generated modules;
- the judge's grades and evidence for every module and section;
- the calibration review sheets and the human grades;
- the computed statistics.


The identifiers of the sandbox cloud accounts (AWS account, GCP project and Azure subscription) are replaced with placeholders wherever they appear; the release lists every redacted file. Results are licensed under CC BY 4.0.


To reproduce one cell:


```text
uv run inspect  eval   src/iacbench/task.py@generate_module -T fixture=G002 \
--model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5 --epochs 3
uv run iacbench judge --grade --samples 3 --fixture G002 \
--candidates <collected modules> --model anthropic/claude-opus-5-5


```
